problem_context: A single isolated +5 nC point charge sits at the origin in otherwise empty space. Point P is located 0.20 m to the right of the charge, and there is nothing physically present at P — no other charge, just empty vacuum. The student is asked: is there an electric field at point P, and if so, what is it?
student_initial_response: So the source charge definitely sets up a field, I get that part. But at point P specifically there's nothing there — no charge sitting at P — so I don't think there's actually a field AT that point. The field is real where the +5 nC charge is, but at P it's just empty space, so there's no field there until you actually put a charge at P for the field to push on. The field kind of only exists once there's a charge to feel it, right?
misconception_description: Student conflates electric field with electric force, not understanding that the field exists independently of any test charge.

knows: a source charge creates an electric field around it
the field is stronger nearer the source charge
the formula E = kQ/r^2 for a point charge's field magnitude
struggles_with: treating the field as existing independently of any test charge
distinguishing the field (a property of space) from the force (which requires a charge to act on)
interpreting E = F/q as defining a field that is there even when q = 0

transfer_problem: Consider Earth's gravitational field at a point 300 km above the ground, where an empty region of space contains no satellite, no astronaut, nothing. Is there a gravitational field at that empty point? If a 2 kg sensor were later placed there, what determines the force it would feel — and was the field already present before the sensor arrived?
transfer_success_criteria: Student asserts the gravitational field exists at the empty point regardless of whether anything is there, because Earth (the source) establishes g throughout the surrounding space. The force on the 2 kg sensor (F = mg) only appears once mass is placed there, but the field g = F/m was already defined and present. A successful transfer explicitly parallels the electric case: the source establishes a field everywhere, the field is a property of space, and the force is a separate quantity requiring an object to act upon.

expert_strategy.diagnosis: The student has correctly grasped that a source charge creates a field but conflates the field with the force it would exert, so they believe the field 'turns on' only when a test charge is present to feel it. The root is reading E = F/q as 'field requires a force, force requires a charge at the point,' rather than understanding the field as a property the source assigns to every point in space independent of any test charge.
expert_strategy.recommended_approach: anchoring_conception leveraging the student's correct 'source creates a field' idea, plus socratic_questioning to separate field from force
scaffolding_sequence: Anchor on what the student already accepts: the +5 nC source creates a field — ask them how far out that field reaches and whether it stops abruptly at any boundary.
Pose the consistency probe: if the field exists right next to the charge in empty space, what is special about point P that would make the field vanish there, given P is also just empty space?

Distinguish the two quantities by definition: introduce E = F/q and ask what E equals at P before any charge is placed — guide them to see E is computed from the source (kQ/r^2), not from the absent test charge.

Run a thought experiment: place a tiny test charge at P, compute the force, then halve the test charge and halve it again — show the force changes but F/q stays fixed, so that ratio (the field) was a fact about P all along.
Bridge to the gravitational field as a familiar analogue: Earth's g exists above the ground whether or not anything is there to fall, framing field as a property of space.
Have the student restate that the field at P exists independently and compute E = kQ/r^2 at P, explicitly separating 'field is present' from 'force appears only when a charge is placed there.'
common_pitfalls: Just giving the formula E = kQ/r^2 and the numerical answer, which the student can plug into while still believing the field only 'really' exists where a charge feels it.
Overcorrecting and dismissing the student's valid partial understanding that the source creates the field, instead of building on it as the anchor.
Letting the test-charge language reinforce the conflation — failing to make explicit that the test charge probes a field that is already there, rather than creating or activating it.
